analysis.one_liner: Toughens federal mine safety law with higher penalties, independent investigations, and new protections for coal miners.
analysis.headline: The mine safety bill died in a House committee without a hearing or a vote, never reaching the House floor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal mine safety law after a decade in which mine disasters killed dozens of miners. It raises fines for safety violations, makes company officers personally liable for knowingly allowing dangerous practices, gives miners new rights to refuse dangerous work and to speak to investigators without their boss's lawyers present, and requires independent investigations of any accident that kills three or more miners. It also tightens standards meant to prevent coal dust explosions, requires real-time air monitoring in underground mines, and makes operators pay miners their full wages when the government shuts a dangerous mine area.
analysis.who_benefits: Underground coal miners and their families. The bill strengthens the right to refuse work that a reasonable person would believe is hazardous, bans retaliation for reporting safety problems, and guarantees up to 60 days of full pay when miners are idled by a safety withdrawal order — under current law, that guarantee is capped at one week. It also gives injured or killed miners' families a role in accident investigations and speeds up black lung medical reports.

how_it_helps.text: Requires an independent investigation, with subpoena power, into any mine accident involving three or more deaths, so the causes are examined outside the operator's influence and outside the Labor Department's own chain of command.

Lets any miner or employee talk privately to federal investigators without the operator or the operator's attorneys present, and protects miners from being fired for refusing work they reasonably believe is hazardous.

Raises civil penalties to as much as $220,000 for specific violations like unauthorized ventilation changes, missed rock dusting, and tipping off mines before inspections, and creates criminal penalties including up to 10 years in prison for operators who knowingly expose miners to serious risk of death.

Guarantees miners full pay for up to 60 days when a withdrawal order closes a mine area, instead of the current one-week cap, and bars mines with chronic violation patterns from firing hourly miners without a legitimate job-related reason.

Raises the required incombustible content of mine dust from 65 percent to 80 percent to reduce explosion risk, requires atmospheric monitoring systems in underground mines, and adds a one-hour annual training on miners' legal rights plus a toll-free hotline for reporting hazards.

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators, who would face higher fines, doubled penalties while in pattern-of-violations status, personal civil and criminal liability for directors and officers who knowingly order unsafe conduct, and new compliance costs for air monitoring, rock dusting, recordkeeping, training, and certified personnel. Those costs are partly passed to coal customers and coal-dependent communities.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on operators, including expensive atmospheric monitoring systems, direct-reading dust monitors, higher training hours, certification fees, and new electronic recordkeeping — costs that hit smaller mines hardest and would be passed into coal prices.

The bill makes directors, officers, and agents personally liable for civil and criminal penalties when they knowingly order or carry out unsafe conduct, which industry argues goes well beyond corporate-level accountability and could deter qualified executives from serving.

Several provisions — doubling penalties, mandating monitors within fixed deadlines, and requiring withdrawal orders for unpaid fines — shift significant discretion to the Labor Department, and operators contend that leaves too little room for genuine disputes over what constitutes a violation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The human stakes — mine explosions and collapses that kill miners in single events — are the kind of harm this bill targets directly: independent investigations, private interviews with investigators, higher fines for the exact violations that preceded past disasters, and real pay for miners idled by safety closures. The main cost is compliance spending by operators, some of which would reach coal customers. The bill was not narrowly tailored to only the worst operators — most provisions apply across the industry — but the core tradeoff, more enforcement against chronic violators in exchange for higher operating costs, weighs in favor of the workers whose lives are on the line underground.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to a subcommittee three months later, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller (D-CA) introduced the Robert C. Byrd Mine Safety Protection Act of 2013 on March 21, 2013, with 17 original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce, where it sat without a markup or hearing; on July 8, 2013 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections.
The bill attracted 28 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never advanced past the subcommittee referral before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators are better off: they continue operating under the pre-existing penalty structure, pay levels, and investigation rules, with none of the new liability, monitoring, or training costs. Miners gained nothing from the bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal operators, who avoided new penalties and rules

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — the sponsor and all 28 cosponsors were House Democrats — and no Republican action moved the bill at any point in the two years it was pending.

industries.note: The bill sharply raises fines for specific safety violations, doubles penalties for mines with chronic violation patterns, adds personal liability for company officers, and requires costly air monitoring, rock dusting, and training. Operators' savings on penalties and compliance come directly at the expense of the safety protections miners would have gained.

industries.industry: Mining equipment and monitoring technology manufacturers
industries.note: Mandatory atmospheric monitoring systems, direct-reading dust explosibility monitors, and electronic recordkeeping requirements would create a new market for safety equipment sold to every underground coal mine.

Higher compliance costs would be passed into coal prices, but the same communities have historically borne the human cost of mine disasters; safer mines mean fewer dead breadwinners and fewer orphaned black lung claims.
